lessons.title: Data Factory vs. SSIS vs. Fabric Data Factory

slots.practicalActivity: In the Azure portal, sketch (on paper or in a doc) where Data Factory would sit in a pipeline moving data from an on-premises SQL Server into a cloud data warehouse, labeling which parts are the E, T, and L, and noting one reason you'd reach for ADF over SSIS or Fabric Data Factory for this specific scenario.
slots.deliverable: A one-paragraph written comparison naming the ETL/ELT split for your sketched scenario and the specific reason ADF (not SSIS or Fabric) fits it.

slots.practicalActivity: Create a real Azure Data Factory instance in your Azure subscription (or free trial), then open Data Factory Studio and visit each hub in turn: Author, Monitor, Manage, and Learning Center, noting what lives in each one.
slots.deliverable: A provisioned Data Factory instance visible in the Azure portal, plus a short note listing all four Studio hubs and one thing you found in each.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter practice: in your new Data Factory instance, create an empty pipeline named Chapter1_Practice, rename it descriptively, and add a single annotation describing what it will eventually do, matching the project-organization habits shown in the Studio tour.
slots.deliverable: One saved, descriptively named, annotated pipeline (still empty) inside your Data Factory instance, confirmed visible in the Author hub's factory resources tree.

lessons.title: Connecting to Azure SQL & On-Premises SQL Server

slots.practicalActivity: Create two real Linked Services in your Data Factory: one to an Azure Blob Storage account (or Azurite/local storage emulator) and one to an Azure SQL Database or local SQL Server instance, testing the connection on each before saving.
slots.deliverable: Two working, connection-tested Linked Services (Blob Storage and SQL) visible in the Manage hub's Linked services list.

slots.practicalActivity: Build one Dataset on top of each Linked Service from the previous slot (a Blob file and a SQL table), import their schemas, then parameterize the SQL dataset's table name and the Blob dataset's file path so both can point at different objects at pipeline-run time.
slots.deliverable: Two datasets with imported schemas, each exposing at least one parameter, confirmed by manually running a quick preview with a different parameter value plugged in each time.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter practice: add a second Blob file and a second SQL table to your source systems, then reuse the same two parameterized datasets from the previous slot (no new datasets) to preview data from the new objects purely by changing parameter values.
slots.deliverable: A short note confirming the same two datasets successfully previewed data from two different underlying objects each, purely through parameter changes, with no new datasets created.

slots.practicalActivity: Build a pipeline with a single Copy activity moving data from your Blob dataset into your SQL dataset, using Auto create table on the sink since the destination table doesn't exist yet, then open the mapping tab and manually adjust one column mapping to confirm you understand how mapping overrides the default.
slots.deliverable: A working pipeline with one Copy activity, run successfully in Debug mode, that auto-created its destination table and shows a manually adjusted column mapping in the mapping tab.

lessons.title: Web, Wait, Fail & Set Variable Activities

slots.practicalActivity: Extend the Copy pipeline with a Lookup activity that retrieves a row count from a control table, a Set Variable activity that stores that value, and a Wait activity, chaining them with the Copy activity into one end-to-end pipeline that runs start to finish without manual steps.
slots.deliverable: A single end-to-end pipeline combining Lookup, Set Variable, Wait, and Copy activities, run successfully in Debug mode with the Lookup's output value visible in the Set Variable activity's input.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter lab: without new instruction, build one original pipeline from scratch that chains at least three Chapter 3 activities together - e.g. Lookup -> Copy (with mapping adjustments) -> Stored Procedure - solving a single realistic scenario such as checking a watermark value, copying only newer rows, and logging the result via a stored procedure.
slots.deliverable: One original pipeline combining at least three Pipelines & Activities chapter techniques into a coherent, successfully executing run, with a short annotation describing the scenario it solves.

slots.practicalActivity: Add a pipeline parameter and a pipeline variable, then build an If Condition activity that branches based on the parameter's value, and a ForEach activity that iterates over a hardcoded array of three table names, calling a Copy activity once per table name inside the loop.
slots.deliverable: A pipeline with one parameter, one variable, a working If Condition branching correctly on the parameter, and a ForEach loop that copies data for all three table names, confirmed by three successful Copy activity iterations in the Debug output.

slots.practicalActivity: Build a parent pipeline that uses Execute Pipeline to call the ForEach pipeline from the previous slot, then add an Until activity that polls a Lookup activity's result and loops until a condition built with the expression language (referencing a system variable like @pipeline().RunId) evaluates true.
slots.deliverable: A parent pipeline that successfully calls the child pipeline via Execute Pipeline and contains a working Until activity whose exit condition references at least one system variable, confirmed by watching it loop at least twice before exiting.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter practice: refactor the parent/child pipeline pair into a single orchestrator pipeline that combines If Condition, ForEach, and Execute Pipeline together to handle a realistic branching scenario, such as looping over tables but skipping any table name matching a parameter-driven exclusion list.
slots.deliverable: One orchestrator pipeline where the If Condition correctly skips the excluded table name during the ForEach/Execute Pipeline loop, confirmed by a Debug run showing the skip in the activity log.

lessons.title: What Is a Mapping Data Flow?

slots.practicalActivity: Turn on Data Flow Debug Mode and create a new, empty Mapping Data Flow, adding a Source transformation pointed at one of your existing datasets, and use the Data Preview tab to confirm real rows are flowing through before adding any transformation logic.
slots.deliverable: A new Mapping Data Flow with Debug Mode enabled and one working Source transformation whose Data Preview tab shows real rows from your source dataset.

slots.practicalActivity: Extend the data flow with a Sink transformation targeting a new staging table, then insert a Filter transformation to drop rows below a threshold, a Select transformation to drop two unneeded columns, and a Derived Column transformation that computes one new calculated column.
slots.deliverable: A data flow with Source -> Filter -> Select -> Derived Column -> Sink, run once via a pipeline's Data Flow activity, with the staging table showing the filtered row count and the new calculated column populated correctly.

slots.practicalActivity: Add a second Source to the data flow and a Join transformation combining it with the first stream, feed the joined output through an Aggregate transformation computing a grouped total, then branch the result with a Conditional Split into two sinks (above/below a value threshold), and in a separate test data flow, Pivot one column's distinct values into new columns.
slots.deliverable: A data flow demonstrating a working Join, an Aggregate producing grouped totals, and a Conditional Split loading two separate sink tables correctly, plus a second small data flow showing a successful Pivot transformation.

slots.practicalActivity: Open the data flow's Optimize tab on the Sink transformation, switch partitioning from Use current partitioning to a specific partition count, re-run the pipeline's Data Flow activity, and compare the run duration and partition count shown in the Monitor hub's data flow execution details against the default run.
slots.deliverable: A short written comparison of two Data Flow activity runs (default vs. custom partitioning) noting the duration and partition count difference observed in the Monitor hub.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter review lab for Mapping Data Flows: build one original data flow from scratch chaining at least four of this chapter's transformations - e.g. Source -> Filter -> Derived Column -> Join -> Aggregate -> Sink - solving one realistic problem such as enriching transaction rows with a lookup stream and summarizing totals by category, then tune its partitioning before the final run.
slots.deliverable: One original Mapping Data Flow combining at least four chapter transformations into a single successfully executing pipeline, with a short annotation describing the business problem solved and the partitioning setting chosen.

slots.practicalActivity: Create a Schedule trigger on one of your existing pipelines set to run daily at a specific hour with a weekday-only schedule narrowing, then create a separate Tumbling Window trigger on another pipeline with a 15-minute window size, and publish both.
slots.deliverable: Two active triggers visible in the Manage hub - a Schedule trigger with a weekday narrowing and a Tumbling Window trigger with a defined window size - each confirmed to have fired at least once in the trigger run history.

slots.practicalActivity: Create a Storage Event trigger that fires your Copy pipeline whenever a new blob is created in a specific container path, test it by uploading a file, then build a Tumbling Window dependency chaining a second pipeline's trigger to only fire after the first window's trigger succeeds.
slots.deliverable: A Storage Event trigger confirmed to fire a pipeline run after a real file upload, plus a Tumbling Window trigger dependency confirmed in the Monitor hub to wait for its upstream window before running.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter practice: review the trigger run history for all four triggers created this chapter in the Monitor hub, and for each one, write one sentence identifying which of the three trigger types it is and why that type fit the scenario better than the other two.
slots.deliverable: A short written note identifying all four triggers built this chapter by type (Schedule, Tumbling Window, or Event-based) with a one-sentence justification for each choice.

slots.practicalActivity: Open the Manage hub's Integration runtimes list, inspect the default AutoResolveIntegrationRuntime, then create a second Azure Integration Runtime pinned to a specific region and compute type, and point one Copy activity at it explicitly instead of the default.
slots.deliverable: A second, explicitly region-pinned Azure Integration Runtime visible in the Manage hub, with one Copy activity confirmed (via its activity run details) to have executed using it instead of the default.

slots.practicalActivity: Create a Self-Hosted Integration Runtime in the Manage hub, download and install the integration runtime software on your own machine (or a local VM) using the generated authentication key, and confirm it shows Running/connected in the Studio.
slots.deliverable: A Self-Hosted Integration Runtime showing a Running, connected status in the Manage hub, installed and authenticated on your own machine.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter practice: build a Linked Service to a local SQL Server instance on your own machine that explicitly uses the Self-Hosted Integration Runtime from the previous slot, then run a Copy activity pulling data from that local SQL Server into a cloud sink, confirming in the activity run details which integration runtime actually executed it.
slots.deliverable: A successful Copy activity run moving data from a local, on-premises SQL Server into a cloud sink, with the activity run details confirming the Self-Hosted Integration Runtime (not the Azure IR) performed the copy.

slots.practicalActivity: In the Monitor hub, review the pipeline and trigger run history built so far, drilling into one run's Gantt view and activity-level details, then configure a retry policy (count and interval) on one Copy activity and set up an Azure Monitor alert rule that fires on pipeline failure.
slots.deliverable: A Copy activity with a configured retry count/interval, plus a working Azure Monitor alert rule for pipeline failures, confirmed by viewing the alert rule's configuration in the Azure portal.

slots.practicalActivity: Add a failure-path activity (connected via the red/Fail precedence) to one pipeline that writes error details to a logging table when the Copy activity fails, deliberately break the source connection to trigger it, then configure a diagnostic setting sending Data Factory logs to a Log Analytics workspace and query the failed run with a simple KQL query.
slots.deliverable: A pipeline with a working failure-path error handler proven by a deliberate failure, plus a Log Analytics workspace receiving Data Factory diagnostic logs, confirmed by a KQL query returning that same failed run.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter practice: pick any three pipelines built earlier in this course and add a consistent monitoring standard to all three - a retry policy on their main activity, a failure-path logging step, and confirm each one's runs are visible together in the Monitor hub's filtered pipeline run list.
slots.deliverable: Three existing pipelines updated with a consistent retry policy and failure-path logging step, confirmed by one filtered Monitor hub view showing successful and/or handled-failure runs for all three.

lessons.title: Dataflow Gen2 vs. Mapping Data Flows

slots.practicalActivity: In a Microsoft Fabric workspace, create a Fabric pipeline and a Dataflow Gen2, comparing the Dataflow Gen2 authoring experience (Power Query-based) side by side with an ADF Mapping Data Flow you built earlier, noting at least two concrete differences.
slots.deliverable: A Fabric pipeline and a Dataflow Gen2, both saved in a Fabric workspace, plus a short written comparison listing two concrete differences from ADF's Mapping Data Flow experience.

lessons.title: When to Choose ADF vs. Fabric

slots.practicalActivity: Set the Dataflow Gen2's output destination to a Lakehouse table in OneLake, then use Fabric's Import from ADF option to bring one of your earlier ADF Copy pipelines into the Fabric workspace, reviewing what imported cleanly versus what needed manual fixing.
slots.deliverable: A Dataflow Gen2 landing real rows in a OneLake Lakehouse table, plus one ADF pipeline successfully imported into Fabric with a short note on what required manual fixing after the import.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter practice: for the ADF-to-Fabric migration pipeline from the previous slot, document a one-page decision memo stating whether this workload should actually live in ADF or Fabric long-term, citing specific reasons from this chapter (cost model, OneLake integration, team skillset, or existing ADF investment).
slots.deliverable: A one-page written decision memo recommending ADF or Fabric for the migrated pipeline's workload, citing at least three specific reasons from this chapter.

slots.practicalActivity: Create an Azure Key Vault secret holding a connection string, grant your Data Factory's system-assigned Managed Identity access to it via an RBAC role assignment, then update one Linked Service to pull its credential from Key Vault instead of a stored value, and connect the whole factory to a Git repository.
slots.deliverable: A Linked Service authenticating via a Key Vault secret retrieved through the Data Factory's Managed Identity, plus the factory itself connected to a Git repo with the current state committed to a feature branch.

slots.practicalActivity: From your Git-connected factory, publish the feature branch to the adf_publish branch to generate ARM templates, inspect the generated template and parameters files, then sketch (or build, if you have an Azure DevOps project available) a release pipeline stage that would deploy that ARM template into a separate Test Data Factory instance.
slots.deliverable: A published adf_publish branch containing a real generated ARM template and parameters file, plus a written or built release-pipeline stage definition describing how it deploys to a Test environment.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter practice: review every Linked Service built across this course and confirm each credential-bearing one now uses Managed Identity or Key Vault rather than a stored plaintext value, fixing any that don't, then re-publish and confirm the Git history shows the security cleanup as its own commit.
slots.deliverable: Every credential-bearing Linked Service in the factory updated to use Managed Identity or Key Vault, with a dedicated Git commit documenting the security cleanup.

lessons.title: Capstone: Connect & Build the Copy Pipeline

slots.practicalActivity: Define the capstone scope: pick a realistic end-to-end scenario (e.g., ingesting daily sales files from Blob Storage plus a lookup table from SQL into a staging schema), write the business requirements, then build the Linked Services, Datasets, and the first Copy activity moving the raw source data into staging.
slots.deliverable: A one-page capstone requirements document plus a working pipeline with real Linked Services, Datasets, and a successful Copy activity loading raw source data into a staging table.

slots.practicalActivity: Capstone lab session 1: harden the Copy pipeline from the previous slot with a parameterized dataset so it can run against multiple source files/tables without modification, and add a Lookup + Set Variable pair capturing a watermark value for the next session's incremental logic.
slots.deliverable: The capstone Copy pipeline now runs against at least two different source objects purely via parameter changes, and captures a watermark value in a pipeline variable confirmed in the Debug output.

lessons.title: Capstone: Add Control Flow & Error Handling
Capstone: Build the Mapping Data Flow

slots.practicalActivity: Add an If Condition and a failure-path error handler to the capstone pipeline using the watermark variable from the previous session, then build a Mapping Data Flow that cleans and reshapes the staged data (Filter, Derived Column, and a Join or Aggregate) before loading it into a final curated table.
slots.deliverable: The capstone pipeline now branches on the watermark via an If Condition, handles a deliberate failure through an error-path step, and includes a Mapping Data Flow that successfully loads a cleaned, reshaped curated table.

slots.practicalActivity: Capstone lab session 2: stress-test the full capstone pipeline by re-running it against modified source data - new rows, a changed value, and a deliberately malformed row - confirming the control flow, error handling, and Mapping Data Flow each behave correctly before moving on to scheduling and security.
slots.deliverable: A written log of three test runs (new rows, changed value, bad row) against the capstone pipeline noting the actual outcome of each, with any bugs found fixed directly in the pipeline.

slots.practicalActivity: Add a Schedule trigger to run the capstone pipeline daily, switch all its credentials to Managed Identity/Key Vault, add a retry policy and Log Analytics diagnostic logging, then write the README describing the scenario, architecture, and techniques used across the whole capstone.
slots.deliverable: The capstone pipeline now runs on a daily Schedule trigger, authenticates entirely via Managed Identity/Key Vault, logs to Log Analytics with a retry policy configured, plus a completed README describing the full architecture.

slots.practicalActivity: Capstone lab session 3: publish the finished capstone factory via Git to the adf_publish branch, confirm the ARM template reflects every component built, then review the Monitor hub's full run history for the capstone pipeline end to end, fixing anything that doesn't pass cleanly.
slots.deliverable: A successfully published capstone factory with a generated ARM template matching the final build, plus a clean Monitor hub run history for the capstone pipeline with no unresolved failures.

slots.practicalActivity: Capstone lab session 4: rehearse a 3-5 minute end-to-end demo of the finished capstone pipeline running live in Debug mode and via its Schedule trigger, walking through the architecture diagram, the data flow logic, the security setup, and the Monitor hub results as if presenting to a hiring manager.
slots.deliverable: A rehearsed, timed (3-5 minute) live demo of the capstone pipeline running end to end, ready to show in an interview or portfolio, alongside the architecture README from the previous lesson.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After completing this course, a student can design, build, and operate real Azure Data Factory pipelines end to end - connecting to cloud and on-premises sources, orchestrating control flow, transforming data with Mapping Data Flows, scheduling and securing production runs, and migrating workloads to Fabric Data Factory where it fits - culminating in a portfolio-ready capstone pipeline.
